categories.name: Universal Questions
categories.description: Asked at nearly every interview — have polished answers ready.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.tip: Not your resume. Lead with what you care about, then connect it to what you do. 60–90 seconds.
questions.avoid: Reciting your activity list or starting with 'I was born in...'

questions.question: Why this school?
questions.tip: Name a specific program, professor, or campus resource. Generic praise ('great academics') is a red flag.
questions.avoid: Rankings, prestige, or anything you could say about any school.

questions.question: What do you want to study, and why?
questions.tip: Connect your interest to a specific experience. Show the path from curiosity → action → deeper question.
questions.avoid: Claiming you've 'always known' or being vague about why.

questions.question: What's your favorite extracurricular?
questions.tip: Pick one where you can describe a specific challenge you solved. Impact > title.
questions.avoid: Listing all of them or choosing one just because it sounds impressive.

questions.question: What do you do for fun?
questions.tip: Be genuine. Reading, cooking, hiking — anything that shows you're a real person, not an application machine.
questions.avoid: Trying to make your hobbies sound like leadership experiences.

questions.question: Is there anything else you'd like us to know?
questions.tip: Use this to address a gap, add context, or reinforce your spike. Don't waste it on 'No, I think we covered everything.'
questions.avoid: Repeating something you already said.

categories.name: Academic & Intellectual
categories.description: Schools want to see genuine curiosity, not performance.

questions.question: What book, article, or idea changed how you think?
questions.tip: Pick something specific and explain what shifted. The quality of your reflection matters more than the title.
questions.avoid: Picking a book you think sounds smart but didn't actually finish.

questions.question: What's a topic you could talk about for hours?
questions.tip: This is your spike question. Go deep — show the interviewer you've genuinely explored it.
questions.avoid: Surface-level answers or picking something generic like 'politics.'

questions.question: What's a class that challenged you?
questions.tip: Show intellectual honesty. How did you adapt? What did you learn about how you learn?
questions.avoid: Making it sound like you easily overcame it. Struggle is the point.

questions.question: How do you approach a problem you've never seen before?
questions.tip: Walk through a real example. Break down your thought process step by step.
questions.avoid: Vague generalities like 'I research it and ask for help.'

categories.name: Community & Impact
categories.description: How you show up for others — not just what you've achieved.

questions.question: How have you contributed to your community?
questions.tip: Community can be your family, school, neighborhood, or online space. Focus on consistent, specific impact.
questions.avoid: One-time volunteer events or listing service hours.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone.
questions.tip: Show you can disagree respectfully and learn from it. The resolution matters more than being right.
questions.avoid: Making the other person the villain.

questions.question: What would your friends say about you?
questions.tip: Be honest and specific. 'She's the one who always has a plan B' is better than 'They'd say I'm hardworking.'
questions.avoid: Listing adjectives without evidence.

questions.question: Describe a time you failed.
questions.tip: Real failure, real lesson. Admissions wants to see resilience and self-awareness, not a humble-brag.
questions.avoid: 'I worked too hard' or any failure that's actually a success.

categories.name: School-Specific Deep Dives
categories.description: Expect these if the school has a distinctive culture or curriculum.

questions.question: How would you take advantage of [school's] open curriculum / core curriculum?
questions.tip: Research the actual course catalog. Name 2–3 courses and explain why they interest you.
questions.avoid: Not knowing what kind of curriculum the school has.

questions.question: What would you bring to [school's] community?
questions.tip: Be specific about what you'd start, join, or change. Connect it to your actual interests and skills.
questions.avoid: Generic 'diversity of thought' answers without substance.

questions.question: Why not [rival school]?
questions.tip: Show you've thought about fit, not just prestige. Focus on what this school offers that others don't.
questions.avoid: Badmouthing other schools.

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in 10 years?
questions.tip: Show direction without being rigid. 'I want to work at the intersection of X and Y' is better than a specific job title.
questions.avoid: Saying 'I don't know' without any follow-up.

categories.name: Curveball Questions
categories.description: Designed to test how you think on your feet. There's no right answer.

questions.question: If you could have dinner with anyone, living or dead, who would it be?
questions.tip: Pick someone connected to your interests. Explain what you'd ask them and why it matters to you now.
questions.avoid: Picking someone just to sound intellectual.

questions.question: What would you do with a free year — no school, no obligations?
questions.tip: Your answer reveals priorities. It's okay to include rest alongside projects.
questions.avoid: Making it sound like you'd spend the year padding your resume.

questions.question: What's something most people believe that you think is wrong?
questions.tip: Pick a genuinely contrarian view you can defend thoughtfully. Show independent thinking.
questions.avoid: Controversial for the sake of being controversial.

questions.question: Teach me something in 5 minutes.
questions.tip: Pick something you know deeply and can explain simply. The skill is communication, not the topic.
questions.avoid: Picking something too complex to explain or too basic to be interesting.

tips: Prepare 5–6 anchor stories that cover different dimensions (academic, community, challenge, leadership, passion). Mix and match for any question.
Research the interviewer if you can — many are alumni who volunteer. Knowing their background helps you ask better questions.
Prepare 3–4 genuine questions to ask at the end. 'What's something you wish you'd known as a freshman?' is better than anything about rankings.
Practice out loud, not just in your head. Record yourself and listen back — you'll catch filler words and realize where you're vague.
Dress one step above your school's dress code. Business casual works everywhere.
Arrive 5 minutes early. Bring a copy of your activity list for reference (don't read from it).
Send a brief thank-you email within 24 hours. Mention one specific thing from the conversation.
